title: NASA Pathways Internship Program 2027: Launch Your Career with NASA Through the Spring 2027 Internship
summary: The NASA Pathways Internship Program offers students an opportunity to gain meaningful professional experience while working with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration. Designed as a long-term talent-development pathway, the program provides multi-semester internship experiences intended to prepare students for careers at NASA and can provide a direct route to full-time employment after graduation. For students interested in science, engineering, technology, communications, public relations, business, administration, information technology, social sciences, and other fields, NASA Pathways can provide an opportunity to apply academic knowledge in a professional environment while contributing to NASA s mission. The Spring 2027 NASA Pathways Internship application window is scheduled to open on September 21, 2026, and close on September 25, 2026. Successful applicants will begin their Spring 2027 internships on January 25, 2027. NASA Pathways Internship Program 2027 NASA strategically recruits Pathways interns based on their long-term potential and alignment with the agency s future workforce requirements. Unlike short-term internship opportunities, the Pathways program specializes in multi-semester experiences that are designed to help students develop the knowledge, skills, and professional experience necessary for future employment. The program is therefore more than an opportunity to spend a few months at NASA. It is structured as a career-development pathway, allowing students to gain experience, receive professional development, work on meaningful assignments, and potentially transition into NASA employment after completing their academic program. NASA describes the program as an opportunity for students who are passionate about its mission and interested in contributing to work connected with exploration, innovation, science, technology, and the advancement of humanity. Spring 2027 NASA Pathways Application Deadline Applications for the Spring 2027 Pathways Internship cycle will open on: Opening date: September 21, 2026 Deadline: September 25, 2026 Internship start date: January 25, 2027 Applicants should pay close attention to the short application window. NASA states that links to the relevant USAJOBS vacancies will be added to the Spring 2027 positions listings when applications open on September 21, 2026. Prospective applicants are encouraged to research available positions and NASA center locations before the application period begins so that they can identify opportunities that correspond with their academic major, professional interests, and preferred geographic location. What Does the NASA Pathways Internship Offer? The NASA Pathways Internship Program is designed around long-term professional development rather than simply providing students with temporary workplace exposure. As a Pathways intern, students can expect to be given challenging and meaningful assignments connected to their academic or career interests. NASA also emphasizes learning, growth, and the development of a supportive professional community. The experience can include: Meaningful work related to the intern s academic or career interests. Opportunities for lifelong learning and professional growth. Exposure to NASA s working environment and organizational culture. Professional assignments designed to develop practical skills. Training and learning opportunities. Opportunities to work toward clearly defined career goals. Development of an Individual Development Plan. Potential consideration for employment with NASA after graduation. The program gives interns a degree of autonomy in defining their career trajectory. Rather than simply completing assigned tasks, participants work with NASA to develop an Individual Development Plan that helps establish assignments, training events, and learning opportunities relevant to their career objectives. Career Opportunities After Graduation One of the most significant features of the NASA Pathways Internship Program is its potential connection to employment after graduation. Throughout the internship, NASA evaluates the intern s experience and, as the student approaches graduation, may consider the individual for full-time permanent employment or term employment lasting between one and six years. Importantly, NASA states that interns who are considered for such employment do not need to submit an additional job application. This makes the Pathways program particularly valuable for students who want to build a long-term career with NASA. The internship provides an opportunity to demonstrate capabilities and develop experience within the agency while still completing an academic program. However, participation in the internship should not be interpreted as an automatic guarantee of employment. NASA states that interns are evaluated as they approach graduation and may be considered for permanent or term employment. Academic Fields and Disciplines Available NASA offers Pathways opportunities across a broad range of disciplines. The specific disciplines and skill sets recruited may vary by application cycle, and NASA posts the specific vacancies before applications open. The occupational classifications listed for the program include areas in engineering, physical sciences, business, communications, administration, information technology, mathematics, statistics, and related fields. Engineering, Science and Technology Opportunities listed in this area include: GS-899: Engineering GS-1399: Physical Sciences These areas may be relevant to students pursuing academic programs connected with engineering, physical sciences, scientific research, and related technical disciplines. Business and Related Fields NASA also lists a broad range of business and professional occupational classifications, including: GS-0099: Safety and Occupational Health GS-199: Social Sciences GS-299: Human Resources GS-399: Administration and Program Management and Analysis GS-599: Accounting and Budget GS-1099: Communication and Public Relations GS-1199: Procurement and Contracts GS-1599: Mathematics and Statistics GS-2299: Information Technology The inclusion of Communication and Public Relations is particularly significant for students studying communications, public relations, strategic communication, media, or related fields. The availability of a specific discipline, however, depends on the vacancies posted for the particular recruitment cycle. What Type of Students Does NASA Look For? NASA states that it seeks students who are captivated by its vision, mission, and core values and who demonstrate characteristics that contribute to the agency s success. The agency emphasizes that its strongest candidates are well-rounded students from a variety of backgrounds. NASA identifies several qualities it looks for in Pathways candidates, including: Curiosity Team orientation Excellence Passion for exploration Agility Resilience An important point for prospective applicants is that prior professional experience is not required . Instead, NASA assesses applicants through seven non-technical competencies: Attention to Detail Flexibility Interpersonal Skills Learning Problem Solving Self-Management (Achievement) Technology Application Students should therefore consider how their academic work, projects, teamwork, leadership activities, problem-solving experiences, and other accomplishments demonstrate these competencies. NASA Pathways Internship Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy NASA s stated eligibility requirements to participate in the Pathways Internship Program. All Pathways interns must: Be a U.S. citizen . Be at least 16 years old . Be enrolled or accepted for enrollment on at least a half-time basis at an accredited educational institution and maintain at least half-time enrollment as defined by that institution. Be pursuing a degree or certificate . Have and maintain a cumulative 2.9 GPA on a 4.0 scale . Be able to complete at least 480 hours of work before completing their degree or certificate requirements. Sign a Pathways Participant Agreement . Undergo a pre-employment background investigation . There is also a Selective Service requirement for certain male applicants. Male applicants born after December 31, 1959, must certify that they have registered with the Selective Service System or that they are exempt under the Selective Service Law. In addition, individual vacancies may establish requirements concerning when applicants must be available to begin work. NASA states that vacancies typically require applicants to be available to begin during a predetermined period, generally within the subsequent two semesters following the closing date of the vacancy. Applicants should therefore review the individual vacancy carefully because requirements can differ depending on the position. Where Are NASA Pathways Internships Located? NASA operates multiple centers across the United States, with different facilities involved in different areas of work. The Pathways program offers opportunities associated with NASA centers located across the nation. Because each vacancy can involve different locations, applicants are encouraged to research NASA s facilities before applying. When submitting an application, candidates should identify vacancies that align with both: Their academic major; and Their preferred geographic location or locations. This approach helps ensure that applicants are considered for work corresponding to their educational background and professional interests. How to Apply for the NASA Pathways Internship The NASA Pathways application process requires applicants to conduct research, prepare an appropriate application, and apply to an eligible vacancy during the specified application period. Step 1: Research NASA Facilities and Opportunities Before applying, applicants should research the types of work performed at NASA facilities. Understanding the activities and responsibilities of different NASA centers can help applicants determine which locations and opportunities best correspond with their academic background and career interests. NASA provides information about its centers and facilities to help prospective applicants make informed decisions. Step 2: Prepare Your USAJOBS Profile and Resume Applicants should visit USAJOBS.gov and create a profile if they do not already have one. After creating the profile, applicants must build or upload their resume. NASA emphasizes that the resume is an important part of the application because it gives candidates an opportunity to explain their background and demonstrate what distinguishes them from other applicants. Applicants should make sure that their resumes are clear, concise, and relevant to the vacancy. A particularly important requirement is that resumes submitted through USAJOBS must be two pages or fewer . NASA states that resumes longer than two pages will be automatically rejected. NASA recommends using the USAJOBS resume builder to help applicants include relevant information while following the required format. Applicants are also encouraged to consult NASA s Pathways Applicant Guide for additional information about the application process, assessment, and hiring procedures. Step 3: Apply During the Open Window Once applications open, applicants should select a vacancy that corresponds with both their academic major and preferred geographic location. For the Spring 2027 cycle, the application window is scheduled for September 21 through September 25, 2026 . Applicants should not wait until the final day if they can submit earlier. Preparing the USAJOBS profile, resume, academic information, and other required materials in advance can make the application process more manageable. NASA s Policy on Artificial Intelligence in Applications Applicants should pay particular attention to NASA s policy concerning artificial intelligence tools. NASA explicitly prohibits candidates from using ChatGPT or other artificial intelligence or AI-assisted tools when creating narrative responses for the employment application and assessment. Candidates are required to create their own original responses and must not plagiarize, copy, or adapt responses from other sources. NASA states that information provided during the application process may be subject to verification and that it may discontinue a candidate s candidacy if it determines that the candidate violated the prohibition on AI tools. This means applicants should ensure that all narrative responses submitted as part of the NASA Pathways application are genuinely their own work. APPLY HERE Preparing a Strong NASA Pathways Application Although NASA emphasizes that previous experience is not required, applicants can still strengthen their applications by presenting their academic background and experiences clearly. Candidates should consider how their experiences demonstrate the competencies NASA assesses. For example, applicants can review their academic projects, group assignments, research, volunteer activities, leadership responsibilities, extracurricular activities, or other experiences and identify evidence of: Careful attention to detail. Ability to adapt to changing circumstances. Effective interpersonal communication. Willingness and ability to learn. Practical problem-solving ability. Self-management and achievement. Appropriate use of technology. Applicants should also make sure that their resume is tailored to the vacancy rather than submitting a generic document that does not clearly demonstrate alignment with the position. Why the NASA Pathways Program Is Significant The NASA Pathways Internship Program stands out because it combines academic study with structured professional experience at one of the world s best-known space and aeronautics organizations. The multi-semester structure gives students the opportunity to develop experience over a longer period, while the Individual Development Plan helps connect internship assignments, training, and learning opportunities with longer-term career objectives. The possibility of being considered for NASA employment after graduation also makes the program particularly relevant to students who are interested in establishing careers within the agency. For students in communications and public relations, social sciences, administration, information technology, engineering, physical sciences, mathematics, human resources, procurement, accounting, and other listed fields, the program can provide a pathway for applying academic knowledge in a professional government environment. Visit HERE for more information about the NASA Pathways Internship Program 2027. Important Dates for Spring 2027 Prospective applicants should take note of the following dates: Applications open: September 21, 2026 Application deadline: September 25, 2026 Internship begins: January 25, 2027 NASA indicates that USAJOBS application links for the relevant Spring 2027 positions will be added to the listings when applications open on September 21. Final Thoughts The NASA Pathways Internship Program provides students with an opportunity to gain meaningful experience while developing toward a potential career with NASA. Its multi-semester structure, professional development opportunities, Individual Development Plan, and potential pathway to employment after graduation make it more than a conventional short-term internship. The program is open to eligible U.S. citizen students who meet NASA s educational, academic, age, work-hour, and other requirements. Opportunities span numerous disciplines, including engineering, physical sciences, social sciences, communications and public relations, human resources, administration, accounting and budget, procurement, mathematics and statistics, information technology, and safety and occupational health. Students interested in the Spring 2027 cycle should prepare ahead of time because the application window is short. Creating a USAJOBS profile, preparing a compliant two-page-or-less resume, researching NASA centers, identifying suitable vacancies, and reviewing the application requirements before September 21 can help applicants be ready when applications open. Most importantly, applicants should carefully follow NASA s instructions concerning original application responses and the use of artificial intelligence. Candidates are responsible for ensuring that their submitted materials comply with NASA s stated application rules. For students who meet the eligibility requirements and are interested in building a career connected to NASA s mission, the Spring 2027 Pathways Internship represents a significant opportunity to gain practical experience, develop professional competencies, and potentially progress toward future employment with the agency. title: Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge 2026: Apply for US$500,000 to Prepare Youth for an AI-Driven Future
summary: The Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge 2026 is inviting eligible nonprofit organizations to submit proposals for innovative programmes that prepare low-income young people for employment in an increasingly artificial intelligence (AI)-driven economy. Through its fourth Global Innovation Challenge, the Citi Foundation is committing US$25 million in total funding to support approximately 50 community organizations , with each selected organization expected to receive a restricted grant of US$500,000 . The initiative focuses on helping young people develop relevant AI, digital, and human-centred skills, improve access to technology, connect with employment opportunities, and strengthen existing youth employability programmes. It is designed to support organizations developing practical, scalable, and innovative solutions that promote economic mobility for low-income youth. The Letter of Inquiry (LOI) deadline is October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. New York Time (Eastern Time) . Opportunity Overview Opportunity: Fourth Global Innovation Challenge: Preparing Youth for AI Funder: Citi Foundation Funding Type: Restricted grant Total Funding: US$25 million Expected Number of Grantees: Up to 50 organizations Expected Grant Amount: US$500,000 per selected organization Grant Duration: 24 months Expected Grant Start: No earlier than June 1, 2027 Primary Beneficiaries: Low-income youth, primarily ages 15 to 24 Eligible Applicants: Registered nonprofit organizations Geographic Scope: Select countries and communities where Citi has a presence First-Stage Application: Letter of Inquiry LOI Deadline: October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time Expected LOI Decision Notification: By the end of November 2026 Expected Final Funding Decisions: No later than the end of May 2027 The application and announcement timelines are subject to change. Applicants should consult the official Citi Foundation Request for Proposals documentation for the latest information before submitting. About the Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge The Citi Foundation’s Global Innovation Challenge is a philanthropic funding initiative that supports community organizations developing innovative responses to major social and economic challenges affecting low-income communities. The 2026 edition focuses on preparing youth for the changing world of work. As AI and digital technologies increasingly influence recruitment, job roles, workplace productivity, and business operations, young people need access to both technical and human-centred capabilities. The Foundation recognizes that low-income youth may face significant barriers to participating in the AI-enabled economy. These barriers can include: Limited access to reliable internet connectivity. Inadequate access to computers, smartphones, and digital tools. Gaps between existing education or training and emerging labour-market needs. Limited exposure to AI technologies. Lack of employment networks and career guidance. Insufficient opportunities to gain practical experience. Unequal access to training in digital and human-centred skills. The challenge therefore seeks to support nonprofit organizations that can develop or expand solutions addressing these barriers and helping young people become more prepared for employment. The Foundation’s announcement states that the challenge will support programmes that combine AI and digital capabilities with skills such as critical thinking, creativity, adaptability, resilience, and problem-solving. These complementary skills are important because young people will need more than technical knowledge to use AI responsibly and effectively in the workplace. Why Preparing Youth for AI Matters Artificial intelligence is transforming industries, job functions, recruitment practices, and the skills employers seek. While AI creates new opportunities, it can also deepen existing inequalities if young people from low-income communities lack access to the tools and training required to participate. The challenge is based on the understanding that youth employability in the AI-driven economy requires a combination of: Technical AI literacy Digital access Practical workplace readiness Human-centred skills Career and employment support Responsible and ethical use of technology The Foundation’s Request for Proposals highlights the importance of helping youth understand, guide, interpret, and apply AI tools rather than simply teaching technical concepts in isolation. The programme is particularly relevant for organizations working with young people who are underserved by traditional education, training, technology, and employment systems. Focus Areas of the Global Innovation Challenge The Citi Foundation identifies three major focus areas for potential proposals. Organizations may develop projects within one or more of these areas, provided their solutions align with the overall goal of preparing low-income youth for employment. 1. Cultivating AI and Human-Centric Skills for Youth Employment The first focus area supports programmes that help low-income youth develop AI-related and human-centred skills relevant to the workplace. Potential activities may include training in: AI fundamentals. AI literacy. Ethical considerations in the use of AI. Prompt engineering. Digital content creation. AI-enabled workplace tools. Digital productivity. Problem-solving. Critical thinking. Advanced reasoning. Creativity. Adaptability. Resilience. Communication and collaboration. The Foundation is interested in approaches that connect technical AI skills with broader employability capabilities. For example, a programme might teach young people how to use AI tools for research, content creation, data analysis, job applications, or business operations while also helping them develop judgment, creativity, communication, and problem-solving skills. Strong proposals should demonstrate how the training will lead to practical employment outcomes, such as improved job readiness, access to work opportunities, stronger career pathways, or better alignment with employer needs. 2. Expanding Digital Access The second focus area supports solutions that improve young people’s access to digital resources and opportunities. Digital access may involve more than providing internet connectivity. It can also include access to devices, software, safe learning environments, relevant digital tools, and platforms that enable young people to participate in the digital economy. Potential examples include: Community technology hubs. Shared computer or device facilities. Digital learning centres. Open-source AI tools. Low-connectivity digital platforms. Offline learning resources. Digital literacy programmes. Connectivity solutions. Technology access linked to employment services. Platforms that connect youth to jobs, internships, apprenticeships, or career opportunities. This focus area is especially relevant for communities where young people may have limited or unreliable internet access. According to the supplied RFP, approximately 2.2 billion young people globally lack internet access at home, creating barriers to economic participation and mobility. Proposals should explain how digital access will be connected to meaningful learning, employment, or economic outcomes rather than treating technology distribution as an isolated activity. 3. Building Support for NGO Capacity and Networks The third focus area supports efforts to strengthen nonprofit organizations’ existing youth employability programmes by integrating AI-enabled tools, training, and resources. It also encourages organizations to build or expand partnerships and networks across sectors, including: Education institutions. Nonprofit organizations. Technology companies. Employers. Government agencies. Training providers. Youth-serving organizations. Community groups. Research institutions. Workforce development organizations. Potential activities may include: Integrating AI tools into existing youth employment programmes. Training nonprofit staff to use emerging technologies. Developing shared curricula or resources. Building cross-sector partnerships. Establishing employer networks. Sharing best practices. Creating learning communities. Strengthening monitoring and evaluation systems. Improving organizational capacity to adapt to changing workforce needs. The Foundation is interested in solutions that promote continuous learning and adaptation because AI-related skills and labour-market requirements are evolving rapidly. Funding Amount and Grant Structure The Citi Foundation plans to award up to 50 restricted grants of US$500,000 each , representing a total commitment of US$25 million . The grants are expected to be distributed over a 24-month period. The anticipated disbursement structure is: US$250,000 in Year 1, expected in 2027 US$250,000 in Year 2, expected in 2028 The grant period is expected to begin no earlier than June 1, 2027 . Because the grants are restricted, funding must be used for the specific programme and eligible expenses described in the successful application. Organizations should develop realistic budgets that clearly connect proposed costs to programme activities, outcomes, and implementation plans. Additional Support Beyond the Grant In addition to financial support, the Citi Foundation intends to explore ways to support selected grantees through: Citi employee volunteerism. A learning community. Knowledge exchange. Shared lessons and best practices. Networking opportunities. Capacity-building activities. Opportunities to learn from other grantee organizations. This additional support may help selected organizations strengthen implementation, improve their approaches, and develop relationships with other organizations working on youth employability and AI readiness. However, applicants should understand that these additional forms of support are described as potential opportunities and should not be treated as guaranteed benefits beyond the grant award. Eligible Organizations The opportunity is intended for registered nonprofit organizations that meet the Foundation’s eligibility requirements. To be eligible, an organization must generally meet the following conditions: 1. Focus on Low-Income Communities The organization must demonstrate that its mission or strategic priorities specifically focus on serving low-income individuals or communities. Applicants should be able to explain: Which low-income populations they serve. The barriers faced by their target beneficiaries. How their proposed programme addresses those barriers. Why their organization is well-positioned to deliver the proposed solution. 2. Operate or Deliver Impact in an Eligible Geography The proposed programme must impact at least one of the Foundation’s target geographies. An organization does not necessarily need to be headquartered in one of the listed countries or regions. However, the programme for which funding is requested must benefit communities within the Foundation’s eligible geographic scope. 3. Be Registered as a Nonprofit Entity Organizations must be registered as nonprofit entities under applicable local law. For example, U.S.-based applicants must generally be tax-exempt public charities under Section 501(c)(3) of the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. Organizations that require fiscal sponsorship are not eligible for this specific funding opportunity. 4. Have the Required Financial Documentation Organizations invited to the full application stage must be able to provide externally audited financial statements covering at least part of calendar year 2024 or a subsequent year by the anticipated application deadline in early December 2026. The audited financial documents must include: An auditor’s signed letter. Complete financial statements. Auditor’s notes. Organizations that cannot meet this requirement should carefully review the eligibility rules before submitting an LOI. Learn More HERE Target Countries and Geographic Eligibility The Citi Foundation’s target geographies cover selected countries and communities across several regions where Citi has a presence. Africa Eligible countries listed in the RFP include: Algeria Cameroon Côte d’Ivoire Democratic Republic of the Congo Egypt Gabon Ghana Kenya Morocco Nigeria Senegal South Africa Tanzania Tunisia Uganda Zambia Asia Pacific Eligible countries and territories include: Australia Bangladesh Hong Kong Indonesia Japan Malaysia New Zealand South Korea Philippines Singapore Sri Lanka Taiwan Thailand Vietnam Europe Eligible countries include: Austria Belgium Bulgaria Czech Republic Denmark Finland France Germany Greece Hungary Ireland Italy Luxembourg Netherlands Norway Poland Portugal Romania Slovakia Spain Sweden Switzerland Ukraine United Kingdom Middle East Eligible countries include: Bahrain Israel Jordan Kazakhstan Kuwait Lebanon Pakistan Qatar Saudi Arabia Türkiye United Arab Emirates Latin America and the Caribbean Eligible countries include: Argentina Bahamas Brazil Chile Colombia Costa Rica Dominican Republic Ecuador El Salvador Guatemala Honduras Jamaica Panama Paraguay Peru Trinidad and Tobago Uruguay North America The RFP lists: Canada Mexico Select regions of the United States The eligible U.S. locations include selected counties, cities, states, territories, and regions in places such as California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, New Jersey, New York, Nevada, South Dakota, Virginia, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico. Organizations should review the official geographic eligibility table carefully because eligibility in the United States is limited to the specific locations identified in the RFP. Can Organizations Based Outside the United States Apply? Yes. Organizations based outside the United States may apply directly if they meet the eligibility requirements and propose programmes that impact one or more of the Foundation’s target geographies. For organizations based outside the United States, grants may be administered through Charities Aid Foundation America (CAF America) . CAF America may request additional information or documentation after the Citi Foundation recommends an award. CAF America will ultimately make the final approval decision for grants to organizations based outside the United States and will have oversight responsibility during the grant term. Application Process The Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge will use a competitive, two-stage application process. Round 1: Letter of Inquiry Interested organizations must first submit a Letter of Inquiry (LOI) through the Foundation’s grant portal . The LOI is intended to help the Foundation assess whether the organization and proposed programme align with the goals of the Global Innovation Challenge. The Foundation will review submissions based on factors including: Strategic alignment. Feasibility. Potential for impact. Organizational eligibility. Relevance to low-income youth. Innovation and practicality of the proposed solution. Alignment with the AI and workforce-readiness focus. Round 2: Full Grant Application The Foundation aims to notify organizations by the end of November 2026 whether they will be invited to submit a full grant application. Organizations invited to Round 2 will receive additional instructions regarding: The full application process. Required documents. Detailed programme information. Budget requirements. Monitoring and evaluation expectations. Submission deadlines. Grant terms and conditions. An invitation to submit a full application does not guarantee funding. It is only an invitation to continue in the competitive process. Final funding decisions are anticipated to be communicated to recipient organizations no later than the end of May 2027. Learn More and Apply HERE Application Deadline The deadline to submit the initial Letter of Inquiry is: October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. New York Time, Eastern Time. Applicants should convert the deadline to their local time zone and submit well in advance of the closing time. The anticipated timeline is as follows: Stage Expected Timeline Global Innovation Challenge launched September 9, 2026 Letter of Inquiry deadline October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time Notification regarding Round 2 invitations By the end of November 2026 Anticipated full application deadline Early December 2026 Expected final funding decisions No later than the end of May 2027 Earliest expected grant start June 1, 2027 Grant disbursement period 2027 and 2028 Grant duration 24 months The Foundation notes that application and announcement timelines may change. How to Prepare the Letter of Inquiry The LOI is the first opportunity for an organization to communicate its programme concept to the Foundation. Applicants should use it to present a clear, compelling, and evidence-informed explanation of the proposed solution. A strong LOI should clearly address the following areas: 1. Define the Problem Explain the specific barriers low-income youth face in the target community or geography. For example, the problem may involve: Limited access to digital devices. Low AI literacy. Lack of employment-focused training. Skills mismatches. Limited access to employers. Inadequate career guidance. Poor connectivity. Lack of opportunities to practise digital skills. The problem statement should be specific rather than relying only on broad statements about AI or youth unemployment. 2. Describe the Proposed Solution Explain what the organization intends to implement, improve, pilot, or scale. The proposal should clarify: What the programme will do. Who it will serve. Where it will operate. How it will work. Why the approach is innovative. How it differs from existing programmes. What makes it practical and scalable. 3. Explain the AI and Human-Centric Skills Connection The programme should demonstrate how it will prepare young people for employment in an AI-influenced economy. Applicants should explain whether the programme will provide: AI fundamentals. Prompt engineering. Digital content creation. AI-enabled tools. Digital literacy. Critical thinking. Creativity. Problem-solving. Communication. Adaptability. Resilience. Ethical and responsible technology use. 4. Identify Expected Outcomes Applicants should explain how they will measure progress and impact. Potential outcomes may include: Number of youth trained. Number of youth gaining digital or AI skills. Number of participants completing training. Number of participants accessing employment opportunities. Number of youth placed in jobs, internships, or apprenticeships. Improvements in digital literacy. Improvements in job-readiness skills. Increased access to devices or connectivity. Employer partnerships established. Increased income or economic mobility. Improved organizational capacity. 5. Demonstrate Organizational Readiness The Foundation will want to understand whether the organization has the experience, staff, partnerships, systems, and resources needed to deliver the proposed programme. Applicants should be prepared to demonstrate: Relevant programme experience. Knowledge of the target community. Qualified staff. Implementation capacity. Financial management systems. Monitoring and evaluation capacity. Partnerships and stakeholder relationships. Experience serving low-income populations. Eligible Expenses Funding will be restricted to the programme and expenses defined in the application. Potential eligible expenses may include: Staff salaries. Technology. Programme materials. Training activities. Events. Research. Communications. Marketing. Monitoring and evaluation. Convenings. Overhead. Other programme-related costs approved under the grant terms. Applicants should ensure that every budget item is clearly connected to programme implementation and intended outcomes. Regranting and Partnerships Organizations may include regranting in their proposed programme budget if there is a clear programme rationale and implementation plan. Regranting refers to redistributing part of the Foundation’s funds to another organization, including local affiliates. Vendor payments for goods or services are not considered regrants. Organizations may also work with partners. However, a single lead organization must submit the LOI on behalf of the partnership. If a partnership advances to the full application stage and is selected for funding: The lead organization will receive the grant. The lead organization will be responsible for the full grant award. The lead organization will be responsible for programme deliverables. The lead organization must ensure that partners comply with the Foundation’s grant terms. Organizations should agree in advance on roles, responsibilities, governance, financial arrangements, and accountability. Important Restrictions Applicants should be aware of several restrictions associated with the grant. No Fiscal Sponsorship Organizations that require a fiscal sponsor are not eligible to apply for this specific opportunity. No Political or Lobbying Activities Grant funds cannot be used directly or indirectly for political or lobbying purposes. This includes activities such as: Participating in or intervening in political campaigns. Supporting or opposing political candidates. Voter registration activities. Get-out-the-vote activities. Independent expenditures supporting or opposing political parties or candidates. Attempting to influence legislation or legislative bodies. One LOI per Organization Eligible nonprofit organizations may submit only one LOI. Separate organizations should not submit multiple LOIs for the same programme. Local affiliates that are separate legal entities and independently meet the eligibility requirements may apply directly, but the same programme should not be submitted more than once by different entities. English-Language Submission LOIs must be submitted in English. Organizations invited to the full application stage must also submit their applications in English, subject to any specific exceptions stated in the application form. No Individual Applications Individuals and sole proprietorships are not eligible applicants. The funding is intended for qualifying nonprofit organizations. Organizations That Will Not Be Considered The RFP identifies several types of organizations and programmes that will not be considered, including: Private foundations, whether operating or nonoperating. Organizations that unlawfully discriminate on protected grounds. Lobbying organizations. Political causes and campaigns. Political candidates. Memorials. Gift-matching initiatives. Organizations requiring fiscal sponsorship. Organizations that do not meet the stated eligibility requirements. Individuals. Sole proprietorships. Applicants should review the complete official terms and eligibility requirements before investing significant time in preparing their submission. Financial Reporting and Grant Accountability Selected grantees will be required to submit: Interim reports during the grant period. A final report through the Foundation’s online grant portal. These reports are expected to demonstrate programme progress, use of funds, implementation achievements, challenges, lessons learned, and outcomes. Organizations should therefore have appropriate systems for: Financial tracking. Programme monitoring. Beneficiary data management. Outcome measurement. Documentation. Reporting. Compliance with grant conditions. Practical Tips for Applicants Organizations considering this funding opportunity can strengthen their preparation by following these recommendations: Confirm eligibility early. Verify nonprofit registration, target geography, low-income community focus, and financial documentation requirements. Choose a specific problem. Avoid presenting a broad proposal about AI. Clearly identify the employment or digital-access challenge affecting the target youth population. Connect AI skills to employment. Explain how training will help participants obtain jobs, internships, apprenticeships, entrepreneurial opportunities, or other meaningful economic pathways. Combine technical and human-centred skills. Include capabilities such as critical thinking, creativity, adaptability, communication, problem-solving, and ethical judgment. Demonstrate community relevance. Use evidence, local data, beneficiary insights, employer feedback, or programme experience to show that the proposed solution responds to a real need. Build practical partnerships. Consider partnerships with employers, educational institutions, technology providers, workforce agencies, and youth-serving organizations. Prepare a realistic budget. Ensure that proposed expenses are eligible, justified, and connected to measurable programme activities. Plan for scale and sustainability. Explain how the programme could be expanded, replicated, integrated into existing systems, or sustained after the grant period. Prepare audited financial statements early. Organizations invited to Round 2 will need the required externally audited financial documentation. Draft the LOI offline first. The Foundation advises applicants to download the editable PDF version of the LOI, prepare responses offline, and then transfer the answers into the online form. Save a copy of the submission. Once submitted, applicants may not be able to access the content entered into the online form. Save the completed PDF or a copy of the final submission for organizational records. Submit before the deadline. Do not wait until the final minutes, particularly if multiple people must review or approve the LOI. Learn More and Apply HERE Conclusion The Citi Foundation Global Innovation Challenge 2026: Preparing Youth for AI represents a major funding opportunity for nonprofit organizations working to improve youth employability, digital inclusion, and economic mobility. With US$25 million in total funding and expected grants of US$500,000 per selected organization , the challenge seeks innovative solutions that help low-income youth develop AI and digital capabilities while strengthening essential human-centred skills. It also supports efforts to expand digital access and improve the capacity of nonprofit organizations and cross-sector networks. Eligible organizations should ensure that their proposed programmes serve low-income communities, impact at least one target geography, and demonstrate a clear connection between AI readiness and employment outcomes. Applicants must first submit a Letter of Inquiry by October 6, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time . Organizations interested in applying should begin by reviewing the official RFP, confirming their eligibility, developing a focused programme concept, preparing a realistic budget, and gathering the necessary organizational and financial information. A strong application should demonstrate not only innovation, but also feasibility, measurable impact, community relevance, and the capacity to help young people participate meaningfully in the future of work. title: Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowships 2027–28: $3,000 Monthly Funding for PhD Scholars and ABD Researchers in Chicago
summary: The Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowships 2027–28 are now open for applications, offering scholars an opportunity to spend one to two months in residence at the Newberry Library in Chicago, United States, conducting intensive research using the institution’s unique and extensive collections. The fellowship is designed for PhD-holding scholars and PhD candidates who have reached ABD (All But Dissertation) status or its equivalent and whose research requires access to specific materials held in the Newberry’s collections. Successful fellows receive a $3,000 monthly stipend to help cover housing, travel, and other living and research-related expenses associated with their residency in Chicago. The program is particularly valuable for researchers whose work depends on primary sources, rare books, manuscripts, maps, historical documents, and other specialized materials that may be difficult to access remotely. Deadline: December 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Central Time. About the Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowship The Newberry Library is an independent research library in Chicago with millions of historical sources and materials documenting people, cultures, places, and events across time. Its fellowship program provides researchers with the time, resources, and scholarly environment needed to undertake intensive research. Fellows do not simply receive financial support; they also become part of the Newberry s scholarly community during their period of residence. The Short-Term Fellowship program specifically supports researchers who need to examine particular items in the Newberry s collections for a defined scholarly project. Unlike the Newberry s Long-Term Fellowships, which support four to nine months of research, Short-Term Fellows generally spend one month in residence. Certain named fellowships can provide two months of support , depending on the fellowship. For researchers who have identified specific Newberry materials that are essential to their work, this can provide an efficient way to spend concentrated time working directly with those sources. Fellowship Benefits Successful Short-Term Fellows receive several important benefits. 1. $3,000 Monthly Stipend Short-Term Fellows receive $3,000 per month . The stipend is intended to help cover the costs associated with undertaking research in Chicago, including: Housing Travel Living expenses Other costs associated with the research residency The Newberry Library does not provide housing , so fellows are responsible for arranging their own accommodation during their fellowship. 2. One to Two Months of Research Residency The majority of Short-Term Fellowships provide one month of support . However, some specific fellowships provide longer support: Jody Enders Fellowship: 2 months Frances C. Allen Fellowship: 1–2 months Lester J. Cappon Fellowship in Documentary Editing: 1–2 months The exact duration therefore depends on the fellowship for which an applicant is considered. 3. Access to Newberry Collections The central benefit of the fellowship is the opportunity to conduct research directly with materials in the Newberry s collections. Applicants should therefore have a clear reason for needing to consult specific Newberry collection items rather than simply wanting general research time in Chicago. The Newberry has millions of collection items, including materials relevant to areas such as American history and culture, maps and cartography, books, manuscripts, performing arts, and American Indian and Indigenous Studies. 4. Participation in a Scholarly Community Fellows become part of the Newberry s scholarly community during their residency. This creates opportunities to interact with other researchers and engage with the intellectual environment surrounding the library s collections and research programs. For scholars working on specialized historical or humanities research, this environment can provide valuable academic connections and opportunities to develop their work. What Fields of Study Are Eligible? One of the major advantages of the fellowship is that applicants can come from any academic field , provided that their proposed project demonstrates a genuine need to work with materials in the Newberry collection. This means applicants should not assume that they must be studying one particular discipline. Potentially relevant fields may include areas such as: History Literature Cultural studies American studies Indigenous studies Anthropology Sociology Religious studies Philosophy Political history Art history Musicology Theatre and performance studies Linguistics Medieval and Renaissance studies Early modern studies Cartography and the history of maps Archival studies Documentary editing Genealogy Other humanities and related disciplines However, simply belonging to one of these disciplines does not automatically make an applicant competitive. The research project itself must demonstrate a specific need to consult Newberry materials . What Makes a Strong Fellowship Project? A strong application should make a clear connection between the applicant s research and the Newberry s collections. Applicants should be able to explain: What they are researching Why the research matters Which Newberry materials they need Why those materials are important to the project What they intend to accomplish during the residency Why the research needs to be conducted in person This is particularly important because the Short-Term Fellowship is not simply a general travel grant. The purpose is to enable scholars to conduct focused research using specific collection items at the Newberry . Applicants should therefore investigate the Newberry s collections and research guides before preparing their proposal. The library provides collection descriptions and research resources to help scholars identify relevant materials. Application Requirements The Newberry processes fellowship applications through its SlideRoom online application portal . The general Short-Term Fellowship application includes several components designed to give reviewers a detailed understanding of the researcher, project, and need for a Newberry residency. 1. Personal, Demographic and Professional Information Applicants will need to provide personal and professional information relevant to their academic or research background. This can include information concerning: Academic institution Academic rank or professional position Department PhD-granting institution Date of PhD award Previous fellowships Previous Newberry fellowship applications or awards Current PhD candidates should provide their anticipated completion date where applicable. 2. Research Project Information The research project is one of the most important parts of the application. Applicants should clearly explain the proposed project and establish the relationship between the project and the Newberry s collections. A strong proposal should demonstrate that the applicant has done sufficient preliminary research to identify the materials they need to consult. The Newberry advises applicants with questions about its materials to contact its librarians. 3. Selective Secondary Source Bibliography Applicants are required to submit a one-page selective secondary-source bibliography related to or contextualizing their research project. This should demonstrate that the applicant understands the existing scholarship surrounding the proposed research. The bibliography should be submitted in Word or PDF format . 4. Curriculum Vitae Applicants must submit a current CV of no more than five pages . The Newberry provides specific terminology for describing forthcoming publications: In progress: not yet completed or submitted Submitted: currently under review Accepted: contracted for publication and undergoing revision In press: with a copy editor, typesetter, or printer Applicants should therefore make sure their CV accurately represents the status of their publications. 5. Fellowship Duration Requested Applicants will indicate how many months of support they are requesting. The majority of Short-Term Fellowships provide one month, while certain fellowships may support two months. 6. Letter of Recommendation One letter of recommendation is required for Short-Term Fellowship applicants. The recommendation should address: The scholarly contribution of the proposed project The value of a Newberry residency to the applicant The applicant s qualifications The recommendation must be submitted in English. Importantly, recommendation letters may be submitted for up to 10 days after the fellowship application deadline . For the 2027–28 cycle, the stated deadline for recommendation letters is December 14, 2026 . Fellowship Period and Timing Awards can be taken at any point within the 15-month period between June of the awarding year and August of the following year . This provides successful fellows with some flexibility when planning their research residency. However, applicants should carefully plan their proposed dates around: Collection access Research needs Academic schedules Housing availability Travel arrangements The Newberry s operating schedule The Newberry notes that fellowship orientations occur on Tuesdays and that the library is closed on Sundays and holidays, while Special Collections and other reading rooms are closed on Mondays. Special Short-Term Fellowship Opportunities In addition to the general short-term fellowship funding, the Newberry offers several fellowships with specific eligibility or research preferences. John S. Aubrey Fellowship This fellowship supports scholars who demonstrate a specific need to use the Newberry s collections. It is therefore one of the general opportunities potentially available to researchers across fields. Lester J. Cappon Fellowship in Documentary Editing This fellowship supports researchers working on historical editing projects that are being prepared for scholarly editions. It is specifically open to postdoctoral scholars and can provide one or two months of support . Jody Enders Fellowship The Jody Enders Fellowship supports exceptional scholars at any career stage whose projects relate to: Medieval theatre Renaissance theatre Other live art forms Rhetoric Translation Preference is given to projects focused on areas outside Britain. This fellowship provides two months of support . Fellows Fellowship The Fellows Fellowship supports scholars who demonstrate a specific need for the Newberry s collections. Preference is given to early-career scholars in all fields whose research relates to: Women s studies Spirituality Venice Applicants do not necessarily need to be working directly in these areas to be considered for the broader Short-Term Fellowship program. Society of Mayflower Descendants in the State of Illinois Fellowship This fellowship supports projects relating to: Early American history Transatlantic history It is another example of how the Newberry s named fellowships can provide targeted opportunities within the broader Short-Term Fellowship program. Fellowships with Additional Membership Requirements Some Newberry Short-Term Fellowships have additional eligibility requirements. Midwest Modern Language Association Fellowship This fellowship supports scholars who: Are members of the Midwest Modern Language Association Are working on projects in literary and cultural criticism Applicants must indicate their interest on the Short-Term Fellowship application form, after which the Newberry will confirm membership status with the MMLA. Newberry Center for Renaissance Studies Consortium Fellowships The Newberry Center for Renaissance Studies supports two awards: One for a postdoctoral scholar One for a PhD candidate Projects should focus on: Medieval studies Renaissance studies Early modern studies Applicants must come from institutions participating in the Newberry Center for Renaissance Studies Consortium. Eligible postdoctoral applicants can include full-time faculty members, adjunct faculty, librarians, and curators. Fellowships for Indigenous Scholars The Newberry also offers specialized fellowships for Indigenous scholars. The Frances C. Allen Fellowship and Susan Kelly Power and Helen Hornbeck Tanner Fellowship support scholars who are: Citizens of federally recognized U.S. tribal nations; Documented descendants of federally recognized U.S. tribal nations; or Native Hawaiian individuals. Importantly, research does not have to focus specifically on American Indian or Indigenous Studies for these fellowships. The Frances C. Allen Fellowship supports female scholars and can provide one or two months of support, while the Power and Tanner Fellowship is open to all qualifying scholars and provides one month of support. These are specialized opportunities within the broader Newberry fellowship ecosystem and should not be confused with the general Short-Term Fellowship eligibility. Is the Fellowship Fully Funded? It is important to understand what the $3,000 stipend means. The fellowship provides $3,000 per month , intended to support: Housing Travel Living expenses Other expenses connected to residing in Chicago However, the Newberry does not provide housing . Therefore, applicants should not automatically describe this as a fully funded fellowship covering every possible expense. Instead, it is more accurately described as a funded short-term research fellowship providing a $3,000 monthly stipend . Researchers should prepare a realistic budget, particularly if they are traveling internationally to Chicago. Application Deadline The deadline for the 2027–28 Newberry Library Short-Term Fellowship is: December 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Central Time. Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin the application because the process involves preparing a research proposal, bibliography, CV and securing a recommendation letter. Recommendation letters or other required supporting materials must be submitted no later than December 14, 2026 , according to the Newberry s application guidance. How to Apply Applications are submitted online through the Newberry Library s SlideRoom portal. Apply Here Before applying, prospective applicants should: Review the Short-Term Fellowship eligibility requirements. Explore the Newberry s collections and research guides. Identify the specific collection materials needed for the project. Develop a clear research proposal. Prepare the selective secondary-source bibliography. Update the academic CV to a maximum of five pages. Identify an appropriate recommender. Ensure the recommender understands the scholarly purpose of the proposed Newberry residency. Complete the SlideRoom application. Submit the application before the December 4 deadline. Confirm that the recommendation letter is submitted by December 14. Applicants who have questions about Newberry materials for their project can contact the library s research staff. The fellowship page lists research@newberry.org for fellowship-related questions. Why This Fellowship Is Valuable for Researchers The Newberry Short-Term Fellowship can be especially valuable for researchers whose work depends on primary-source research. A scholar may have a strong research question but need to physically examine historical documents, manuscripts, maps, books, archival records, or other specialized materials that cannot be adequately studied through digital copies or secondary literature. A concentrated residency provides the researcher with dedicated time to: Examine primary sources Take research notes Compare archival materials Verify historical evidence Develop chapters or articles Strengthen a dissertation Prepare a scholarly edition Advance a book project Build relationships with other researchers Develop new interpretations based on primary sources The Newberry describes its broader fellowship program as providing researchers with the time, space and community needed to pursue innovative scholarship. Important Tip for Applicants One of the strongest ways to improve an application is to avoid presenting the fellowship simply as an opportunity to visit Chicago or conduct research at a prestigious library. Instead, demonstrate a specific scholarly need . For example, your proposal should make it clear: My project requires consultation of these particular Newberry collection materials because Then explain how examining those materials will advance your research. Applicants should also research the collections carefully before applying. The Newberry recommends its research guides, bibliographies, checklists and collection descriptions as resources for identifying relevant materials. The more precisely you can connect your research question, the specific collection materials and the expected research outcomes, the stronger the rationale for a short-term residency becomes. Other Newberry Opportunities Researchers who do not meet the Short-Term Fellowship eligibility requirements may still find other Newberry opportunities. Artists-in-Residence Fellowships Writers, artists and other creative researchers who do not hold a PhD or ABD status may be better suited to the Newberry s Artist-in-Residence Fellowship program. NCAIS Fellowships Faculty members and graduate students from institutions affiliated with the Newberry Consortium in American Indian and Indigenous Studies (NCAIS) may qualify for NCAIS fellowships and research awards. These programs have separate application requirements and deadlines. Tribal Research Fellowships Researchers conducting work on behalf of a U.S. federally recognized tribal nation can explore the Tribal Research Fellowship . That program supports individuals or small groups working with federally recognized tribal nations and can provide up to $10,000 depending on the project. Long-Term Fellowships Researchers who need substantially more time may consider the Newberry s Long-Term Fellowships. These provide four to nine months of research support and offer $5,000 per month . Applicants must already hold a PhD at the time of application. The 2027–28 deadline is November 20, 2026. With $3,000 per month in funding , a one- to two-month research residency, access to Newberry collections and participation in a scholarly research community, the fellowship can help researchers make substantial progress on dissertations, books, articles, documentary editions and other scholarly projects. The most important consideration for prospective applicants is the connection between their project and the Newberry s collections. Applicants should identify the specific materials they need, explain why those materials are essential to their research and demonstrate what they expect to accomplish during their residency. The application deadline is December 4, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. Central Time. Recommendation letters may be submitted until December 14, 2026. For researchers whose scholarship depends on primary sources held by the Newberry, this fellowship could provide both the financial support and dedicated research environment needed to take their work to the next stage.
